source_text: Νόμισον εἶναι τὸ πρᾶγμα διαδικασίαν, ὁ μὲν πατήρ σοι δοκείτω παρεστὼς λέγειν ›ἐγώ σε ἔσπειρα καὶ ἔθρεψα, ἀκολούθει μοι καὶ συναδίκει καὶ μὴ πείθου τῷ Χριστοῦ νόμῳ‹ καὶ ὁπόσα ἂν εἴποι βλάσφημος ἄνθρωπος καὶ νεκρὸς τῇ φύσει. ἑτέρωθεν δὲ ἄκουε τοῦ σωτῆρος· ›ἐγώ σε ἀνεγέννησα, κακῶς ὑπὸ κόσμου πρὸς θάνατον γεγεννημένον, ἠλευθέρωσα, ἰασάμην, ἐλυτρωσάμην· ἐγώ σοι παρέξω ζωὴν ἄπαυστον, αἰώνιον, ὑπερκόσμιον· ἐγώ σοι δείξω θεοῦ πατρὸς ἀγαθοῦ πρόσωπον· »μὴ κάλει σεαυτῷ πατέρα ἐπὶ γῆς·« »οἱ νεκροὶ τοὺς νεκροὺς θαπτέτωσαν, σὺ δέ μοι ἀκολούθει·« ἀνάξω γάρ σε εἰς ἀνάπαυσιν καὶ ἀπόλαυσιν ἀρρήτων καὶ ἀλέκτων ἀγαθῶν, »ἃ μήτε ὀφθαλμὸς εἶδε μήτε οὖς ἤκουσε μήτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπων ἀνέβη. εἰς ἃ ἐπιθυμοῦσιν ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι καὶ ἰδεῖν ἅπερ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀγαθὰ καὶ τοῖς φιλοῦσιν αὐτὸν τέκνοις.« ἐγώ σου τροφεὺς ἄρτον ἐμαυτὸν διδούς, οὗ γευσάμενος οὐδεὶς ἔτι πεῖραν θανάτου λαμβάνει, καὶ πόμα καθ᾿ ἡμέραν ἐνδιδοὺς ἀθανασίας· ἐγὼ διδάσκαλος ὑπερουρανίων παιδευμάτων· ὑπὲρ σοῦ πρὸς τὸν θάνατον διηγωνισάμην καὶ τὸν σὸν ἐξέτισα θάνατον, ὃν ὤφειλες ἐπὶ τοῖς προημαρτημένοις καὶ τῇ πρὸς θεὸν ἀπιστίᾳ.‹ τούτων τῶν λόγων ἑκατέρωθεν διακούσας ὑπὲρ σεαυτοῦ δίκασον καὶ τὴν ψῆφον ἀνένεγκε τῇ σαυτοῦ σωτηρίᾳ· κἂν ἀδελφὸς ὅμοια λέγῃ κἂν τέκνον κἂν γυνὴ κἂν ὁστισοῦν. πρὸ πάντων ἐν σοὶ Χριστὸς ὁ νικῶν ἔστω· ὑπὲρ σοῦ γὰρ ἀγωνίζεται.
orientation: Clement is addressing the believer directly, staging a courtroom scene in which the earthly father and Christ each make their case for the believer's allegiance.
pass_a_gloss: Consider the matter to be a legal contest. Let the father seem to you to stand by and say: 'I sowed you and nourished you; follow me and join in wrongdoing and do not obey the law of Christ,' and whatever a blasphemous man and dead by nature might say. But from the other side hear the Savior: 'I begot you again, you who had been badly begotten by the world unto death; I freed you, I healed you, I ransomed you. I will provide you life unceasing, eternal, above the world. I will show you the face of God the good Father. Do not call for yourself a father on earth. Let the dead bury the dead, but you follow me. For I will lead you up into rest and enjoyment of unutterable and unspeakable good things, which neither eye has seen nor ear has heard nor has entered into the heart of humans, into which angels desire to look and to see the good things which God has prepared for the saints and for the children who love him. I am your nourisher, giving myself as bread, of which no one who tastes any longer receives experience of death, and giving daily a drink of immortality. I am teacher of supercelestial lessons. For your sake I contended against death and paid your death, which you owed for your former sins and for unbelief toward God.' Having heard these words from both sides, judge on your own behalf and carry up the vote to your own salvation; even if a brother says similar things, even if a child, even if a wife, even if anyone at all. Before all things let Christ the victor be in you; for he contends for you.

choices.why: The noun denotes a formal legal dispute or trial, matching the courtroom staging Clement sets up with two opposing speakers.
The compound verb means to beget anew or regenerate; the literal 'begot again' preserves the birth imagery Christ uses against the father's 'I sowed you.'
The adjective means supermundane or transcending the world; the literal rendering keeps the spatial contrast with the world that begot the believer unto death.
The noun denotes one who feeds or rears; 'nourisher' preserves the parallel with the father's claim to have nourished, while Christ offers himself as bread.
The verb means to struggle or fight through a contest; 'contended' keeps the athletic and legal contest imagery running through the passage.
The phrase refers to casting a ballot or vote in a legal decision; 'carry up the vote' preserves the courtroom metaphor and the upward direction toward salvation.

pass_b_english: Think of the matter as a legal contest. Let your father seem to stand beside you and say: "I sowed you and nourished you; follow me and join in wrongdoing, and do not obey the law of Christ," and whatever else a blasphemous man, dead by nature, might say. On the other side, hear the Savior: "I begot you again, after the world had begotten you badly unto death; I freed you, healed you, ransomed you. I will give you life unceasing, eternal, above the world. I will show you the face of God the good Father. 'Call no one your father on earth' (Matthew 23:9). 'Let the dead bury their own dead, but you follow me' (Matthew 8:22). For I will lead you up into rest and the enjoyment of good things that cannot be spoken or told, 'things no eye has seen and no ear has heard and no human heart has conceived' (1 Corinthians 2:9), things angels long to look into and see, the good things God has prepared for the holy and for the children who love him (1 Peter 1:12; 1 Corinthians 2:9). I am your nourisher, giving myself as bread, of which no one who tastes any longer experiences death, and daily giving a drink of immortality. I am a teacher of lessons above the heavens. For you I contended against death and paid your death, which you owed for your former sins and your unbelief toward God." When you have heard these words from both sides, judge for yourself and carry up the vote for your own salvation. And if a brother says similar things, or a child, or a wife, or anyone at all, let Christ the victor be in you above all. For he contends on your behalf.

problems.quote: Call no one on earth your father
problems.source_quote: μὴ κάλει σεαυτῷ πατέρα ἐπὶ γῆς
problems.why: Greek says ‘do not call yourself father on earth’, English reverses agency to address others.
problems.fix: Do not call yourself father on earth
problems.ruling: σεαυτῷ = 'yourself'; source says 'do not call yourself father on earth,' not 'call no one...your father.' Agency reversed.

edits.old: Call no one on earth your father (Matthew 23:9).
edits.new: Do not call yourself father on earth (Matthew 23:9).

fixed: Agency reversed: source μὴ κάλει σεαυτῷ πατέρα ἐπὶ γῆς means 'do not call yourself father on earth', not 'call no one on earth your father'.

problems.quote: things angels long to look into and see, the good things God has prepared for the holy and for the children who love him (1 Peter 1:12)
problems.source_quote: εἰς ἃ ἐπιθυμοῦσιν ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι καὶ ἰδεῖν ἅπερ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀγαθὰ καὶ τοῖς φιλοῦσιν αὐτὸν τέκνοις
problems.why: Clement fuses 1 Peter 1:12 (angels long to look) with 1 Cor 2:9 (prepared for those who love him). Attributing the whole clause to 1 Peter 1:12 mislabels the 'prepared' language.
problems.fix: things angels long to look into and see, the good things God has prepared for the holy and for the children who love him (1 Peter 1:12; 1 Corinthians 2:9)
problems.ruling: Greek combines 1 Peter 1:12 (angels long to look) with 1 Cor 2:9 (God prepared for those who love Him); English cites only 1 Peter 1:12.

problems.why: Greek verb ἐξέτισα means ‘I destroyed/abolished’, not ‘paid’. The English changes the sense of Christ’s action.
problems.ruling: ἐξέτισα from ἐκτίω means 'I destroyed/abolished'; 'paid' mistranslates, changing Christ's action from destroying death to paying it.

edits.old: things angels long to look into and see, the good things God has prepared for the holy and for the children who love him (1 Peter 1:12)
edits.new: things angels long to look into and see, the good things God has prepared for the holy and for the children who love him (1 Peter 1:12; 1 Corinthians 2:9)

fixed: wrong_scripture: Clement fuses 1 Peter 1:12 and 1 Corinthians 2:9; added 1 Corinthians 2:9 to the citation.
mistranslation: Greek ἐξέτισα means 'I destroyed/abolished', not 'paid'; changed to 'destroyed your death'.

problems.quote: Do not call yourself father on earth
problems.why: Scripture citation embedded mid-speech without clear attribution; reader may think it is Clement's instruction.
problems.fix: Set off with quotation marks and a clear speaker tag.

edits.old: Do not call yourself father on earth (Matthew 23:9).
edits.new: "Do not call yourself father on earth" (Matthew 23:9).

fixed: The source has μὴ κάλει σεαυτῷ πατέρα ἐπὶ γῆς, which is part of the Savior's speech. The English already renders it as part of the Savior's quoted words, and the quotation marks around the whole speech make the speaker clear. The citation in parentheses is standard for the translation. No edit needed.

last_rejected.why: 1 Peter 1:12 has 'angels long to look' but lacks 'the good things God prepared for the holy and for the children who love him'; that clause is from 1 Corinthians 2:9.

last_rejected.why: συναδίκει means 'join in judging/condemning,' not 'join in wrongdoing.'
last_rejected.ruling: συναδίκει means to collude or be an accomplice; “join in wrongdoing” is acceptable.
